content: Education in dementia care will enhance awareness of the condition, improve diagnostic rates, elevate the quality of care, and foster better integration and coordination of services. This aligns with Action Area 4 of the Global Action Plan on the Public Health Response to Dementia 2017–2025, specifically Indicator 6, which focuses on the dementia health and social care workforce. A well-trained and qualified workforce is essential to deliver high-quality, evidence-based dementia diagnosis, treatment, care, and support. The competencies required for dementia care include a deep understanding of person-centered care, effective communication, collaboration, ethical considerations, evidence-based practices, and cultural diversity. Current evidence suggests that effective training combines classroom instruction, case studies, supervised interactive training, and repeated exposures. Ideally, a national care certificate with minimum training standards, a standardized dementia curriculum, and competency assessments would ensure consistent care across various settings and professions. The estimation of workforce adequacy involves responses from national authorities, such as departments of psychiatry, public health, psychology, social care, nursing schools, and training centers in geriatrics and mental health. Dementia care competencies encompass diagnosis, assessment of comorbidities, management of behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), risk reduction, palliative care, and addressing caregiver distress. Health and social care professionals involved include physicians, neurologists, psychiatrists, geriatricians, nurses, social workers, personal support workers, and pharmacists, among others. Dementia care services must address the complex needs and high dependency levels associated with the later stages of the disease. These services include identification, diagnosis, pharmacological and psychosocial treatment, rehabilitation, palliative/end-of-life care, and support such as home help, transportation, and structured day activities. Integrated, evidence-based, person-centered care is required across all settings, including homes, communities, assisted-living facilities, nursing homes, hospitals, and hospices. Sustainable care requires timely diagnosis, integration of dementia care into primary care, coordinated long-term care, and collaboration between multidisciplinary teams and caregivers. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) play a critical role in empowering individuals with dementia and their families through advocacy and information provision, enabling informed decision-making about care. In many countries, NGOs are the backbone of service delivery for dementia care. Indicators in this domain link to proposed actions in Action Areas 4 and 5 of the Global Action Plan, specifically Indicator 7, which focuses on diagnostic rates for dementia. Diagnosis is the first step in accessing necessary health and social care services. The diagnostic rate for dementia is calculated using the number of diagnosed individuals aged 60 and over as the numerator and the estimated total number of people with dementia in the same age group as the denominator. This can be based on national data or WHO prevalence estimates. Community-based services for dementia include diagnostic services in primary care, management of BPSD, psychosocial services, rehabilitation, daily living support, and palliative/end-of-life care. These services aim to maintain functional capacity, independence, and community living for individuals with dementia. Psychosocial interventions address the ongoing psychological and social needs of individuals with dementia, their caregivers, and families. Palliative care improves the quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illnesses by preventing and relieving suffering through early identification, assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial, and spiritual problems. Social and financial protections, such as government-provided benefits, tax allowances, and subsidized services, support individuals with dementia and their caregivers. The availability and accessibility of community-based services, as well as the major providers (public, private, or both), are critical for effective dementia care. The percentage of individuals with dementia receiving these services is an important measure of service coverage. Health and social care facilities for dementia must meet the complex needs of individuals in the later stages of the disease. Facility availability and capacity indicate the ability to provide care and meet patient preferences. Data on facilities, such as hospitals and residential care centers, are collected by national authorities and international organizations like WHO and OECD.
